e.t: This word is a proper name referring to a person named Abdiel, also identified as Avthil. It is not a general description or action word, but a personal designation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 5:15. The available rendering presents the name as Abdiel, while the lexical identification also gives Avthil as a form of the name. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain that person’s specific role in the passage.

Aimarek, also rendered Emarek, is a proper name for a specific place or location rather than a general word describing an idea, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 19:21. Because the available information identifies the term as a name but does not provide the verse’s wording or a broader definition, its main meaning is simply the designation of that named place. Its precise significance in Joshua depends on the surrounding geographical list and passage context.

This noun refers to unfruitfulness or barrenness—the condition of producing no fruit or useful result. It can describe a lack of fruitfulness in a literal or figurative sense, while the surrounding passage determines its precise force. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears once, in Proverbs 9:12. Its central idea remains the absence of expected fruit or productivity, rather than a particular kind of fruit or a specific cause of barrenness.

Amazonis is a proper name, referring to a specific named person, place, or group rather than expressing a general quality or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Chronicles 14:14. The available lexical meaning identifies it simply as “Amazonis,” so its precise referent must be understood from that passage’s surrounding text. It should therefore be read as a name preserved in the biblical account, not translated as an ordinary descriptive word.

This Greek LXX noun means “going up” or “mounting.” It refers to movement upward or an ascent, describing the act of going from a lower place to a higher one. The word occurs 28 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so it has a recognizable but not extremely frequent use. Its exact force in a passage depends on what is being approached or ascended, but its central idea remains upward movement.

gl: make to step back; call back
d: make to step back; call back

e.t: This verb means “make to step back; call back.” It describes an action that causes someone to step back or brings someone back from moving forward. As a verb, it focuses on reversing another person’s movement rather than simply describing someone who is already standing back. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice: once in Sirach 48:23 and once in 2 Maccabees 14:44. The surrounding verse determines whether the immediate sense emphasizes stepping back or calling back.

This Greek LXX adjective means “without hearing.” It describes someone who does not hear, whether through inability or a failure to listen, depending on the sentence. The word appears five times in the Greek Old Testament, in Numbers, Job, Proverbs, and Jeremiah. Its central idea remains the absence of hearing; the surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on not receiving sound or on refusing to listen. It is distinct here as a Greek LXX word, not a Greek New Testament entity.

This adjective describes something that is opposed, set against another thing, or antithetic to it. It points to contrast rather than agreement, showing that two matters stand in opposition. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Esther and once in Job. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains clear: something contrary or directly opposed to something else.

e.h: Hold Off or Have in Full
e.t: This Greek LXX verb means “hold off” or “have in full.” It can describe keeping something at a distance or possessing and receiving something completely, depending on the sentence. The word occurs 11 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its basic idea appears in more than one setting rather than carrying a narrow, specialized sense. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being held off or fully received.

This Greek LXX verb means “restore” or “pay,” describing the act of returning something, putting something back in its former condition, or giving what is owed. Its central idea is making something right again through return or repayment. It occurs 39 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its exact sense depends on what is being returned or restored in each passage. The word is used across historical, prophetic, and wisdom writings.

This verb means “bring to birth,” describing the act of giving birth or bringing forth new life. It is an action word rather than a title or description of a person. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central meaning remains the act of bringing forth through birth.

Arus is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in 2 Kings 21:19. The available rendering preserves the name as “Arus,” while the lexical definition also gives “Arous” as a form of the name. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the person’s role in that passage.

This adjective describes someone or something as “infirm” or “ailing”—weakened, sick, or lacking strength. It can refer to physical condition and, depending on the sentence, to a state of weakness rather than health or vigor. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 20 times, so its basic sense is established across multiple passages without being limited to one situation. The surrounding verse determines whether the weakness is bodily or expressed more broadly.

This Greek LXX verb means “increase”: it describes becoming greater in amount, extent, or strength. As a verb, it expresses an action or process of growth rather than naming a person, object, or quality. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Job 29:3. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense is growth or increase. This word is a proper name, rendered “Barne” or “Varni.” It identifies a named person or place in the Greek Old Testament tradition rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It occurs 10 times in the LXX corpus, from Numbers through Joshua. Because the supplied information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, its specific referent must be determined from each passage’s context.

Beelim is a proper name, rendered “Beelim” or “Veelim.” It identifies a named place or people rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at Ezekiel 27:4. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the name’s precise referent must be understood from that passage’s context. Its lexical meaning is therefore the name itself: Beelim, also known as Veelim.

This noun means “arm,” referring to the limb extending from the shoulder to the hand. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, it is used 116 times, so it is a well-established ordinary word for the human arm. It can describe an arm in physical actions, positions, or descriptions, but the precise force of any particular occurrence depends on its surrounding verse and passage.

Gaziron is a proper name referring to a particular person or place named Gaziron. It is not presented here as a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented by this record, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 4:15. The name’s precise identification and significance depend on the surrounding passage, which is not included in this lexical entry.

This noun means “nativity,” referring to birth or the circumstances surrounding someone’s being born. It names the beginning of a person’s life rather than a later stage or event. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical corpus, it occurs twice: once in Genesis and once in Sirach. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains connected with birth and origin.

Golgol is a proper name, preserved as “Golgol” rather than translated into a descriptive idea. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, at Deuteronomy 11:30. Because the available lexical information gives only the name itself and no verse text or broader relationship pattern, its exact referent cannot be identified here. The word’s ordinary function is therefore to designate the named entity indicated by that passage, while the surrounding verse supplies the details of what or whom it names.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Dathema” and also identified as “Thathema.” It functions as a name rather than a general description or action word. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 5:9. Because the available lexical information gives names rather than a descriptive definition, its main significance is identifying the named subject in that passage; the surrounding verse is needed to explain the passage’s specific context.

This Greek LXX noun refers to reasoning or an argument—the thoughts, conclusions, or contentions formed in the mind and expressed in words. It can describe ordinary human thinking as well as reasoning directed toward or against someone. The word occurs 19 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including Psalms, Sirach, Lamentations, Isaiah, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any verse depends on whether the surrounding passage presents the reasoning as wise, troubled, proud, or opposed to God.

This word means “two thousand” and functions as an adjective, describing a quantity of two thousand items or people. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 36:8. Its basic meaning is numerical and precise; the surrounding sentence determines what is being counted. The English rendering recorded for that occurrence is shortened, but the stated lexical meaning is “two thousand.”

This word means “seventieth,” describing the person or thing that comes in position seventy in a sequence. It is an adjective, so it normally identifies a numbered place, occasion, or unit rather than naming an object by itself. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs seven times: once in Zechariah and six times in 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the noun or event it describes, but its central meaning remains the ordinal number seventy.

gl: suck the marrow out of; deprive of strength
d: suck the marrow out of; deprive of strength

e.t: This Greek LXX verb means “suck the marrow out of” and, by extension, “deprive of strength.” It describes the action of exhausting something by drawing out its vital substance. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Numbers 24:8. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central picture is clear: strength or substance is drawn out until what is being acted upon is weakened.

This verb means “turn inside out; turn out.” It describes an action of turning something outward or reversing its position, rather than simply leaving it unchanged. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears four times, each in a separate verse. Its occurrences span Deuteronomy, Ezekiel, Amos, and Zechariah, showing that the word can describe a forceful change in how something is arranged or directed. The exact sense in any particular verse depends on what is being turned and the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun refers to a “socket” or to “artificial flowers.” It names a crafted object rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Exodus 38:16, so its use is limited and closely associated with the description of constructed items. The precise sense intended in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and the object being described.

This Greek Old Testament verb means to summon people to an assembly or to convene them together. It describes the act of calling a group to gather, rather than the group itself. In the Septuagint, it appears 19 times across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, showing repeated use for formal or purposeful gatherings. Its meaning remains focused on bringing people together by summons. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun means “elevation,” referring to something being lifted up, raised, or brought to a higher position. It describes the idea of upward movement or heightened standing rather than a specific object by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times across four verses, so its precise force is determined by what is being elevated in each passage. The word appears in Psalms, Lamentations, Ezekiel, and Zechariah, showing its use across different kinds of Old Testament writing.

This Greek LXX verb means “order”: it describes directing someone to do something or establishing what must be done. Its wording presents an authoritative instruction rather than a mere suggestion. The word occurs 20 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek books represented in this corpus, so it is used across several settings involving commands, regulations, or official directions. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on who gives the order and what is being commanded.

This adjective describes something that is plainly visible, apparent, or notable. It can point to what stands out clearly rather than remaining hidden or unnoticed. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish books represented here, the word occurs 10 times, showing a recurring use for people, actions, or conditions that are conspicuous or distinguished. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is being manifest or notable.

This Greek LXX verb means “dispute”: to engage in disagreement, contention, or argument. It describes an action rather than a person or thing, so it points to the act of disputing. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here, across passages from Genesis, 1 Samuel, 2 Kings, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central idea remains entering into dispute or contention.

This Greek verb means “favorable.” It describes expressing or showing favor, functioning as an action or state rather than naming a person, object, or event. Its basic sense is positive disposition toward someone or something, though the surrounding verse determines the specific direction of that favor. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs three times, so its meaning is concise and consistent rather than broadly varied across many passages.

Zachri, also rendered Zakhri, is a personal name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies individuals named in the genealogical and historical records of Chronicles. The name occurs twice in this corpus, once in 1 Chronicles 27:27 and once in 2 Chronicles 17:16. Without the surrounding verse text, these references establish the name’s use but do not provide a further meaning or lesson attached to it.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Ēdad” or “Ithath.” It identifies a particular person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 6:19. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name itself supplies the main meaning: it is a personal designation used in the biblical genealogy or list where it appears.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Ēdin” or “Ithin.” It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament tradition rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It occurs twice in the Greek LXX text, both times in Nehemiah: 7:20 and 10:17. Since the surrounding verse text is not provided here, the name’s specific role in each passage cannot be described further.

Thargal is a personal name used to identify a named individual. It is not presented as an ordinary descriptive word with a separate action, quality, or object meaning. In the Greek Old Testament, the name appears twice, both times in Genesis 14. Its meaning is therefore preserved as the name “Thargal,” rather than expanded into an English definition. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the individual’s specific role in either occurrence.

This adjective means “muddy,” describing something clouded, dirty, or lacking clarity. It is a Greek LXX word found once in the Old Testament Greek text, at Habakkuk 2:15. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s exact force in that sentence cannot be described further. Its central idea remains the condition of being muddied or made unclear, rather than something clean, clear, or transparent.

This Greek LXX noun means “wood,” referring to wood as a natural material or substance. It identifies something made of, obtained from, or associated with trees, rather than expressing an action or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament text represented here, at 1 Samuel 14:25. Its precise significance in that verse is determined by the surrounding passage, but its ordinary lexical sense remains simple and concrete: wood.

Iarib, also rendered Iariv, is a proper name used to identify a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as an ordinary action, quality, or object word, but as a personal designation. In the LXX corpus, it occurs four times, in 1 Chronicles and Ezra. Its precise reference in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

Ithak is a proper name rendered “Ithak.” It identifies a named person, place, or other entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Joshua 15:42. The name itself supplies its identifying function, while the surrounding verse would be needed to determine exactly what or whom Ithak names there. No broader lexical sense is given.

This word means “rainbow,” the visible arc of colors that appears in the sky. It is a noun, naming this natural sign rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, it occurs once, at Exodus 30:24. The word’s basic meaning is clear from its direct definition, while the significance it carries in that verse must be understood from the surrounding passage. This is a Greek LXX word and should be kept distinct from similarly rendered words in the Hebrew or Greek New Testament corpora.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Isaia” or “Isea.” It identifies a named person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Chronicles. The precise person intended in each occurrence depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here. Its meaning is therefore primarily its name-value: Isaia, also represented as Isea in one English rendering.

This word means “jar,” referring to a container used to hold something. It is a noun, so it names an object rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 40:15. The word’s basic sense is therefore straightforward: a jar or vessel considered as a physical container. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its comparison, which are handled separately from the word’s ordinary meaning.

This noun means “standard”—a rule, measure, or recognized norm used for comparison or judgment. It points to something that establishes what is proper, consistent, or acceptable, rather than merely describing an individual object. In this Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice: once in the Old Testament and once in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This noun describes amazement or consternation—a powerful reaction of startled wonder, alarm, or deep disturbance. It names an emotional response rather than an action or object. In the Greek of the Septuagint, it occurs once, in Ezra 3:3. The word’s precise force there belongs to the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning points to a person being overwhelmed or shaken by what has happened or been seen.

This Greek LXX verb means “repair” or “outfit”: it describes restoring something so it is sound or preparing it with what it needs. As a verb, it expresses an action performed on an object, person, or situation rather than naming the thing itself. It occurs 17 times in the Greek Old Testament, especially in Psalms and Ezra, showing use across both poetic and historical settings.

This Greek LXX verb means “take delight in”: to find pleasure in something or regard it with deep enjoyment. It describes an active response of delight rather than merely noticing or approving something. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament represented here, both times in Psalms, at Psalm 36:4 and Psalm 36:11. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the joyful taking of pleasure in something.

This Greek LXX noun means “ark,” referring to a substantial vessel or chest. It is used broadly across the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, occurring 219 times. Its earliest recorded use is in Genesis 6:14, and it also appears in passages such as Exodus 25:14. The word’s ordinary sense remains the same while the surrounding passage identifies what kind of ark is meant.

This word means “helmet” or “helm,” referring to protective armor worn on the head. It is a noun, so it names the piece of equipment itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it appears once, in Wisdom 5:18, and is rendered “helmet.” The word therefore carries a straightforward physical meaning: head protection used as part of armor. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the basic sense remains a protective head covering.

Lasa is a proper name, preserved as “Lasa” in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a specific name rather than a general description or action word. This form occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Genesis 10:19. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, its precise referent cannot be identified here, but the lexical evidence supports treating Lasa as a name, not translating it as an ordinary concept or quality.

This noun means “vegetable,” referring to edible plant food. It names food that grows from plants and is used as part of ordinary nourishment. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times across four verses, including passages in Genesis, 1 Kings, Psalms, and Proverbs. Its precise reference in any one passage depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning remains straightforward: a vegetable or similar cultivated plant food. The word does not itself express a moral quality or spiritual condition; it identifies a kind of food.

Masaias is a personal name, rendered as “Masaias” or “Maseas.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, object, or teaching. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 15:20. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the person’s specific role in that passage cannot be explained from the name alone. Its ordinary function is simply to designate the individual called Masaias or Maseas in that account.

This word describes someone who is high-minded and noble—marked by an elevated, honorable character rather than a petty or mean outlook. It functions as a noun for such a person. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, it occurs three times: once in Proverbs and twice in 4 Maccabees. Its central idea is moral and personal nobility, describing the kind of person whose thoughts and character rise above what is base or dishonorable.

Meramoth is a proper name, rendered “Meramoth,” rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. Its meaning is therefore its identity as a name, not a broader concept that can be translated into an ordinary English definition. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, both times in Nehemiah: Nehemiah 3:21 and Nehemiah 10:6. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the specific reference in either passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “transfer” or “alter”: to move something from one place, position, or condition to another, or to change it. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or fixed quality. The word occurs 17 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented in this corpus, including passages from Genesis, Deuteronomy, Psalms, Proverbs, Isaiah, and the Maccabean books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being moved or changed in the surrounding passage.

This conjunction means “while not” or “nor,” joining words or clauses in a negative statement. It can deny an action, condition, or possibility, and it can connect one negative thought with another. The word appears 131 times in the Greek LXX corpus, showing regular use across its books rather than a meaning limited to one setting. Its exact force in a particular sentence depends on the words and clauses it joins. [p03:word:lxx:L708855:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L708855:occurrences]

This verb means to be engaged or betrothed—formally pledged to marry. It describes a person who has entered an established marriage promise, though the wedding itself has not yet taken place. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 3:56. Its precise force in that sentence depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its ordinary meaning points to a recognized commitment toward marriage.

Mōphaath is a proper name, rendered “Mōphaath” or “Mofaath.” It functions as the name of a specific named entity rather than as a general description, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 6:64. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not provide a further definition or explain the identity of the entity named. Its precise significance in that passage therefore depends on the surrounding verse and list in which the name appears.

“Namouēli; Namoili” is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament, identifying a person named in the biblical text. The name appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at Numbers 26:12. Its lexical entry gives no additional descriptive meaning, action, quality, or title beyond identifying the named individual. Understanding the person’s role or significance requires reading the verse and its surrounding passage, rather than treating the name itself as a common word.

This noun means an island or islands: land surrounded by water. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it refers to such places as geographic locations, including distant coastal lands. The word occurs 39 times in this Greek LXX corpus, with many occurrences in Isaiah and Ezekiel. Its basic meaning remains straightforward, while the surrounding passage determines which island or group of islands is being mentioned.

Othali is a proper name, rendered as “Othali.” It identifies a named individual rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, this name occurs once, in Ezra 10:28. Since it is a personal name, its meaning is chiefly its identifying function: it distinguishes one person from others in the biblical record. The surrounding verse supplies the specific role or context associated with Othali.

This word means “lasting”. It is an adjective describing something by its continuing duration. Depending on the sentence, it can characterize a person, thing, or situation as enduring over time. In the Greek LXX, this word appears once, in Wisdom 9:5. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its exact force in that verse cannot be explained; its basic meaning remains “lasting”.

gl: sharing in the drink-offering; sharing the same cup
d: sharing in the drink-offering; sharing the same cup

e.t: This adjective describes someone or something sharing in a drink-offering or sharing the same cup. It points to participation in a common drink or offering, rather than merely being near it. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 3:7. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s exact force in that sentence must be understood from its context; its basic idea remains shared participation in the cup or offering.

This noun means “use,” referring to the usefulness or practical value of something. It names what something is good for or accomplishes, rather than describing an action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs once, at Job 15:3. Its basic sense is therefore concise: use, usefulness, or practical purpose. The surrounding verse is needed to show exactly how that idea functions in context.

This verb means “head along” or “head aside”—to lead, bring, or direct someone or something from one place or direction toward another. It describes movement guided by an agent rather than merely movement occurring on its own. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scriptures, it occurs 13 times, so its basic sense appears in several settings without becoming a common everyday verb. The surrounding sentence determines whether the emphasis is leading onward or turning aside.

This adverb means “five-fold,” describing something done or given in an amount multiplied by five. It answers the question “how much?” by indicating a five-times measure rather than naming an object or action itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Genesis 43:34. Its exact force in that verse is best understood from the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains a fivefold quantity or proportion.

This noun means “overflow”: an amount that exceeds what is normally contained, needed, or expected. It describes excess or abundance rather than something merely present in an ordinary measure. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 12 times, all within Ecclesiastes, so its usage is concentrated in that book. The surrounding context determines what is overflowing in a particular verse, but the central idea remains an excess that goes beyond the usual measure.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Persēs” or “Persis.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 44 times, appearing especially in Ezra, Daniel, and Esther. Because it functions as a name, its particular personal reference must be determined from the surrounding verse and passage. The name appears from 2 Chronicles through 4 Maccabees within this Greek corpus.

This noun means “brick-making”: the work or process of producing bricks. It refers to an activity rather than to the bricks themselves. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, all in Exodus, where its references belong to descriptions of the labor connected with making bricks. Its basic meaning remains focused and concrete: the manufacture of bricks as a form of work.

This word means “when?”. It is an adverb or particle used to ask about the time of an action or event. In ordinary reading, it points the question toward a time: at what point, or on what occasion, something happens. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times, showing a focused use rather than a broad range of meanings. Its exact force in any sentence depends on the surrounding words, but its central function remains a question about timing.

This verb means “sprout afresh”: to begin growing again after having been cut back, weakened, or apparently finished. It describes renewed growth, using the picture of a plant sending out new life. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 17:9. The surrounding verse is needed to determine precisely how this image functions there, but the word itself centers on fresh growth emerging again rather than merely continuing uninterrupted growth.

This Greek LXX verb means “smile upon.” It describes the act of directing a smile toward someone, functioning as an action word rather than a name or description. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 8:4. Because the verse text is not included here, the specific person involved and the precise force of the action must be understood from that passage’s surrounding context.

This adverb means “from morning,” marking the point from which something begins or continues. It identifies morning as the starting time, rather than naming a person, object, or action. The word occurs ten times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, including passages in Exodus, Ruth, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, Job, and 1 Maccabees. Its exact force in any sentence depends on the action or event connected with it.

This adjective describes something as “fiery red,” emphasizing a vivid color associated with fire. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it appears three times: twice in Ezekiel and once in Sirach. The word functions as a descriptive color term rather than naming an object or action. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and the thing being described.

gl: easiness of temper; taking things easily
d: easiness of temper; taking things easily

e.t: This noun describes an easygoing disposition—being relaxed in temperament and taking things easily. It points to a person’s manner or attitude rather than to a specific action. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, so its broader range cannot be established from repeated uses. Its basic sense is a light, untroubled approach, though the surrounding verse would determine whether that quality is presented positively or as a weakness.

Samch is a noun functioning as a specific name or designation. It is not presented as an ordinary action, quality, or object description, but as the name “Samch” itself. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs only once, at Psalms 118:113. The available lexical information identifies the word but does not provide the verse text or surrounding context, so its precise role in that occurrence cannot be explained further from this word entry alone.

This adverb means “clearly”: in a sentence, it describes something done, stated, seen, or understood plainly and without obscurity. It points to clarity rather than uncertainty or concealment. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, including passages from Deuteronomy, Habakkuk, and the books of Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its ordinary meaning remains straightforward: something is evident, plain, or unmistakable.

Sethennak is a proper name, apparently identifying a place or location rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 15:31, within a list of places belonging to Judah. The name itself is rendered as “Sethennak,” and the available information does not provide a broader lexical meaning beyond this designation. Its precise significance in Joshua depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek LXX verb means to pitch a tent or camp. It describes settling in a place by putting up a tent, whether temporarily or as part of travel and dwelling. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament represented by this entity, across three verses in Genesis and Judges. Its basic sense is practical and physical: establishing a campsite or making a temporary dwelling. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis falls on the act of pitching the tent or on the resulting encampment.

This word means “crown; honour,” describing the act of crowning or honoring someone. As a verb in the Greek Old Testament, it presents honor as something given or placed upon a person, often pictured through a crown. It occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament, including uses connected with Proverbs, Isaiah, and Song of Songs. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “twisted band,” referring to a strip or cord formed by twisting. It names a physical object rather than an action or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach 31:20. Its precise role in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning remains a twisted band. This is a concrete, material term describing something made by winding or twisting strands together.

This Greek LXX verb means “confuse” or “confound”: to make people or circumstances unclear, disordered, or difficult to understand. It describes an act that disrupts clear thought, communication, or expected order. The word occurs 15 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, including passages from Genesis, 1 Samuel, 1 Kings, and Joel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central idea remains the disruption of understanding or order.

This Greek LXX verb means “conspire” or “conclude.” It describes people joining together in an agreement, whether for a secret plan or for reaching a settled decision. The surrounding context determines which sense is intended. It occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, including passages in 1 Samuel, 1 Kings, and 1 Maccabees. Its basic idea is bringing people or matters together through agreement.

This adverb means “vehemently,” describing an action carried out with powerful force or intensity. It tells the reader how something is done rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs four times across Genesis, Joshua, Sirach, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise emphasis in any individual verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its normal function is to strengthen the manner or force of an action.

This Greek verb means “distribute” or “store up.” It describes the action of managing something by either giving it out or keeping it in reserve. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 12:12. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense concerns deliberate handling of what has been entrusted or gathered.

This noun means “keel,” the main supporting structure running along the bottom of a boat or ship. It names a physical part of a vessel rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Wisdom 5:10. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and wider context, but the word itself refers plainly to the keel of a vessel.

This Greek LXX verb means “attain” or describes something as “ordinary.” It can point to reaching or obtaining something, while in another use it characterizes what is usual rather than exceptional. The word appears 22 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented here, so its precise sense depends on how it functions in the sentence. It is found especially in 2 Maccabees, but also appears in Esther, Job, 1 Maccabees, and 3 Maccabees.

This adverb means “soundly” or “fairly,” describing how something is done in a healthy, proper, or just manner. It can qualify an action or judgment, emphasizing that it is carried out rightly rather than carelessly or dishonestly. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears once, in Proverbs 31:8. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains an action performed soundly or fairly.

This Greek LXX noun means “endurance”: the continuing strength to remain steady rather than give up. It describes patient perseverance through difficulty, need, or prolonged waiting. The word occurs 24 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, showing a recurring emphasis on steadfast persistence. Its precise force in any passage depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea remains the ability to continue faithfully under pressure.

Phase is a proper name, rendered as “Phase” and also represented as “Fasi.” It identifies a named individual or group in the Greek Old Testament text rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Ezra 2:49. Without the surrounding verse text, its particular identity or role cannot be described further, but its basic function is clear: it serves as a personal or group designation.

This verb means to enunciate or speak—to express words aloud. In the Greek Old Testament, it describes the act of giving utterance. Its central idea is spoken expression rather than a specific message or emotion. It occurs 14 times in the Greek LXX corpus, across Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. The exact force in any verse comes from its surrounding context.

This word means “pit,” referring to a deep opening or hollow in the ground. It is a noun used for physical places that can hold water, provide access to underground sources, or serve as a dangerous depression. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 59 times, with many uses in Genesis and further appearances across other Old Testament books. Its exact force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding words, but the central idea remains a pit or deep opening.

Phryx, also rendered Friks, is a proper name rather than a descriptive word. It identifies a person or figure by name, but the available information does not include enough surrounding verse text to explain that individual’s role or significance. In the Greek LXX corpus, this name occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 5:22. Its meaning is therefore chiefly its identifying function: Phryx is the name of the one referred to in that passage.

Chebrōni, also rendered Khevroni, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action or quality. It identifies a particular person or group in the Greek Old Testament tradition. The name occurs four times across three verses, appearing once in Numbers and three times in 1 Chronicles. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific referent cannot be described more precisely here, but its lexical function is clear: it serves as a personal or group designation.

This Greek LXX noun means “gall” or “bile,” the bitter fluid associated with the body. It names a physical substance rather than an action or quality. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing once in Ecclesiastes, once in Wisdom, and twice in 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains the bodily substance called gall or bile.

This Greek LXX verb means “be.” It expresses the idea of being or existing, functioning as a verb in a sentence rather than naming a person, object, or quality. Its exact force depends on what is being described in the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains simple: to be. It occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament material represented here, so it is an uncommon word in this corpus.

This verb means “explore” or “survey”—to examine an area carefully, likely by traveling through it and taking stock of what it contains. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in two verses of Joshua 18, where the translation uses “explore” for its repeated use in Joshua 18:8. Its basic sense is active investigation of a territory rather than merely looking at it from a distance.
